paragraphs.text: [Rougui](yancha:rougui), cassia in Chinese, is a Wuyi cultivar from the Qing dynasty, and it is now one of the most widely planted teas in the area. This leaf was made the standard [rock tea](yancha:definition) way: twisted into long thin strips, then finished with a [charcoal roast](yancha:making). The roast is done in several rounds with rests between them, not in one pass, so the leaf dries enough to keep.

The [Wuyi Mountains](wuyi-mountains:where-it-is) run along the border of northern Fujian and Jiangxi. The range is steep and wet, and fog is common there all year. The bushes grow in [thin, stony soil](wuyi-mountains:nature) in the ravines and on ledges. The ground drains fast and the plants grow slowly, and that rock is where the tea gets its name.

brewing.text: Wuyi tea is usually brewed gongfu style with water at or near the boil, about 95 to 100°C, and about 5 to 8 grams of leaf in a 100 to 120 ml gaiwan, a third to a half full. A quick rinse, poured off at once, is common. Steeps start short, about 5 to 20 seconds, and grow a few seconds longer each round, and good rock tea gives seven steeps or more. In a larger pot, use about 2 to 5 grams for 250 to 350 ml and steep two to three minutes.

notice.text: Roast and stone fruit, a mineral, rocky texture and a long, sweet, mouth-watering finish. Light roast is bright and floral, medium roast fruity and rounded, full roast charcoal, wood and roasted nuts. Da Hong Pao is often floral, Rougui spicy with cinnamon, young Shui Xian sweet and smooth, and old-bush Shui Xian woody and mossy.

unsupported.why: No claim says where a name comes from. The claims gloss 岩 as 'rock' and say rock tea grows among rock, but none says the name comes from the rock. This tea's own name, Rougui, comes from the cinnamon-bark smell (yancha:rougui), so the sentence can also be read as wrong about this lot.
